This week the map moved across 14 km of water, three dying rivers and one renamed island.

50,000 people crossed into a Spanish city on the African coast. The Rhine hit a record low. Nauru became Naoero.

5 ways the map moved — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ ~50,000 Moroccans surged into Ceuta last week (NYT). Most left within a day; at least 67 died trying. Von der Leyen has written to Sánchez demanding tougher borders (BBC, Guardian).

Ceuta is 18.5 sq km of Spain in Africa — one of the EU's only land borders there.

2/ Trump says fresh talks are Iran's "last chance" and that Hormuz could reopen "by tomorrow." Iran says it's talking to Oman about the route — not to Washington (BBC, NYT).

BBC: the threat to tankers is the worst since the war began. The detour past Aden isn't safe either.

3/ The Rhine has hit a record low. The Rhine, Danube and Po are all cutting freight and power output (BBC).

Hungary's only nuclear plant ran at ~10% for lack of cooling water, then shut. Romania blew up a rock outcrop to improve flow (DW).

Rivers are infrastructure.

4/ Russian officials say Ukrainian drones killed 11 on the Black Sea coast and in Crimea — 7 on a crowded beach, 3 of them children (BBC, Guardian, NYT). Not independently verified.

BBC also reports strikes near Moscow, Tver and St Petersburg. The war's map keeps widening.

5/ Nauru is now the Republic of Naoero — the spelling and pronunciation used in its own language (Guardian, NYT).

Country code NRU → NRO. Its people are dei-Naoero.

21 sq km of raised coral, strip-mined for phosphate for a century. Every atlas on earth now updates.

The data behind it: Morocco sits several shades darker than Spain on the map of youth not in education, work or training.

NYT found Moroccans in Ceuta describing economic despair, not persecution.

Europe's steepest colour break is 14 km wide.
